title: Moonlight in the Heart
body:
Dear friend,

In Japan, there is an old autumn custom called tsukimi—moon viewing. As the rice ripens in the fields, people look up at the clear night sky and quietly take in the light of the moon.

Hōnen, the founder of Jōdo Shū (the Pure Land school of Buddhism), left us this poem:

Tsukikage no
itaranu sato wa
nakere-domo
nagamuru hito no
kokoro ni zo sumu

"Though the moonlight encompasses the world, its beauty dwells only in those who gaze at the moon."

Moonlight reaches the mountains and the towns. It falls equally upon every roof, every path, and every field. Yet its beauty comes alive in the heart of the person who pauses to look up.

For Hōnen, this moonlight was an image of Amida Buddha’s compassion. That compassion is not a reward reserved for those who have done everything well. It shines upon those who are lost, those who are grieving, and those who are carrying regret or self-doubt. It is already reaching us, quietly and without discrimination.

But in the busyness of daily life, we may forget to look up. Worries fill our minds. We hurry from one task to the next. It can seem as though the light has disappeared. Yet perhaps it has not disappeared at all. Perhaps we have simply lost the stillness needed to notice it.

If you find the moon in the sky tonight, pause for a moment and gaze at it. You may wish to say Namu Amida Butsu—words that mean, "I take refuge in Amida Buddha"—either aloud or silently in your heart.

The moonlight is not shining upon you only from some distant place. When you look up and receive it, it is already dwelling within your heart.
